focus_area: LLM capabilities, emergence, in-context learning, interpretability, and alignment

anomalies.measurement: When linear/continuous metrics (e.g., token edit distance) are used, LLM performance improves smoothly and predictably with scale; the apparent sharp phase transitions disappear entirely.
anomalies.prediction: Scaling law theory and prior empirical reports predicted that LLMs develop qualitatively new capabilities in sharp, unpredictable jumps at certain model scales — genuine emergent phase transitions analogous to physical phase changes.
anomalies.discrepancy: What appeared as sharp emergent phase transitions are not present when measured with linear metrics, meaning the 'emergence' is induced by the researcher's choice of nonlinear/discontinuous metric rather than reflecting a real change in the model's underlying per-token error rate.

anomalies.anomaly_name: The Reversal Curse: Asymmetric Factual Generalization in Autoregressive LLMs
anomalies.measurement: LLMs trained on 'A is B' facts fail to answer 'B is A' queries: GPT-4 answers 'Who is Tom Cruise's mother?' 79% correctly but only 33% for the reverse ('Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son?'); the correct reversed answer scores no higher than a random baseline name.
anomalies.prediction: Standard generalization theory predicts that a model learning a symmetric factual relation (e.g., 'X is the parent of Y') should generalize bidirectionally; basic logical deduction expects 'A is B' training to imply availability of 'B is A'.
anomalies.discrepancy: Models trained on 'A is B' achieve near-zero generalization to 'B is A' (performance no better than chance on reversed queries), despite demonstrating that they can perform this logical deduction when 'A is B' appears in context rather than training data.
anomalies.primary_quote: a surprising failure of generalization in auto-regressive large language models (LLMs). If a model is trained on a sentence of the form "A is B", it will not automatically generalize to the reverse direction "B is A"

anomalies.anomaly_name: Inverse Scaling: Larger LLMs Perform Worse on Specific Tasks
anomalies.measurement: Across 11 empirically identified benchmark tasks, increasing model size from small to 280B+ parameters consistently degrades performance; 10 of these tasks later showed 'U-shaped' scaling when tested up to 540B parameters, meaning performance first drops then recovers only at extreme scale.
anomalies.prediction: The dominant scaling law framework (Kaplan et al., Chinchilla) predicts monotonically improving performance with model size across tasks; larger models were expected to be uniformly better.
anomalies.discrepancy: On identified tasks, larger models are measurably worse than smaller models — a direct violation of the standard scaling law prediction — with causes including preference to imitate undesirable training data patterns and sensitivity to misleading few-shot demonstrations that increase with scale.
anomalies.primary_quote: LMs may show inverse scaling, or worse task performance with increased scale, e.g., due to flaws in the training objective and data

anomalies.anomaly_name: LLMs Know More Than They Show: Internal Truth-Encoding vs. External Hallucination
anomalies.measurement: Linear probes trained on LLMs' internal hidden-state representations can accurately predict whether an output is a hallucination, with truthfulness signals concentrated at specific answer tokens — yet the models still externally generate those incorrect outputs despite internally encoding the correct answer.
anomalies.prediction: The standard model of LLM hallucination assumes that erroneous outputs arise from an absence of correct information in the model's representations; if a model 'knows' the answer, it should output it.
anomalies.discrepancy: A measurable discrepancy exists between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: probes recover correct-answer signals from internal states even when the model's output is a hallucination, meaning the model encodes the right answer but still generates a wrong one.

anomalies.anomaly_name: RLHF Fine-Tuning Degrades Calibration: Aligned Models Are Less Calibrated Than Their Pretrained Bases
anomalies.measurement: RLHF-aligned models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude) exhibit poorly calibrated conditional probabilities and express verbalized overconfidence significantly greater than their unaligned pretrained counterparts; calibration error increases after RLHF even as instruction-following improves.
anomalies.prediction: Standard training theory predicts that additional fine-tuning on human-preferred outputs, which tends to select for correct and helpful answers, should maintain or improve probability calibration relative to the pretrained base.
anomalies.discrepancy: RLHF fine-tuning, despite improving instruction-following and user-rated quality, measurably worsens calibration: models sacrifice well-calibrated probability estimates to better satisfy the reinforcement learning objective of allocating mass to the single most preferred answer rather than matching true answer frequencies.
